resources.string: Say why
Pick the verdict with the right reason.
Without the closing parenthesis, the syntax phase complained. Why not the lexical one?
while (i < 10 i = i + 1;
The tokens exist. The matching parenthesis is missing.
The lexical phase does not read parentheses, only letters and digits.
The lexical phase only finds type errors.
Look at each piece alone. Do the parenthesis, the i and the ten exist?
Every token is fine. The matching parenthesis is missing, and that is the shape of the sentence.
If S were just B, epsilon would go into FIRST of S. Why?
S → B B → C | b C → c | ε\nFIRST(S) = { b, c, ε }
Everything in the rule can vanish: B vanishes through C.
Every FIRST of a nonterminal has ε.
B has ε written in its own rule.
Follow B to the end. Can it turn into nothing?
B becomes C, and C becomes epsilon. With no d after it, the whole rule can vanish.
If Y could never vanish, plus would leave FOLLOW of F. Why?
T → F Y Y → * F Y | ε\nFOLLOW(F) = { *, +, ), $ }
F only inherits FOLLOW of T when Y vanishes.
Plus only comes in through FIRST of Y.
FOLLOW never has the plus.
The plus came from FOLLOW of T. When does F inherit from it?
F inherits from T only when it sits at the end of the rule. If Y never vanishes, that never happens.
R goes to epsilon went only into the dollar column. Why?
L → id R R → , id R | ε\nFOLLOW(R) = { $ }
Only $ comes after R.
A rule with ε always goes in the $ column.
FIRST of R is $.
The epsilon rule goes in the FOLLOW columns. What comes after R?
After R comes only the end of the input. That is why the epsilon rule sits under dollar.
In the state of S goes to id dot, the closure adds nothing. Why?
S → id •
There is no nonterminal after the dot.
A state with a single item has no closure.
The closure only runs in state zero.
The closure looks at the symbol right after the dot. Which one is it?
No symbol is left after the dot. With no nonterminal there, there is no rule to add.
With an open parenthesis after id, the cell stayed empty. Why?
S → id •\nFOLLOW(S) = { ), $ }
( never follows S, and no item waits for it.
An open parenthesis cell is always empty in SLR.
Reducing only counts in the $ column.
Reducing only counts in the columns of FOLLOW of S.
An open parenthesis never comes after S. And no item in the state waits for it.
States three and six became a single state. Why can they merge?
I3: C → c • C , c/d\nI6: C → c • C , $
Without the lookaheads, the items are the same.
Both came from the same state.
Both have the same lookaheads.
Compare the two boxes while covering the lookaheads.
Without the lookaheads, the items are the same. Same core, so they can merge.
In round one, every final state splits from every non-final one. Why?
E is final. A, B, C and D are not.
The empty string accepts in one and rejects in the other.
Final and non-final states have different arrows.
The recipe marks one pair per round.
Reading nothing, one of them already accepts. What about the other?
Reading no letter at all, one accepts and the other does not. The empty string tells them apart.
Here the minus ended up below the times. Why?
total * (preco - 2)
The minus runs first, and the times uses the result.
Minus has higher precedence than times.
Minus always goes below times, in every expression.
Which operation must come out first for the times to work?
The parenthesis says to do the minus first. The times sign uses its result.
Both lw come before the add. Why?
lw lw add sw
The add only works between registers.
The lw is faster than the add.
The order does not matter. It is just habit.
Where can the add get its numbers from?
In MIPS, arithmetic only happens between registers. The lw brings each variable into one of them.
The ++ came out as a single token. Why?
The scanner takes the longest piece that matches.
Two equal symbols always become one token.
Every operator has two characters.
Does the scanner stop at the first plus, or go as far as it can?
Longest match. The ++ matches whole, so it does not become two pluses.
The state after the a is not final. Why?
a b* c
The expression requires the c at the end.
A state in the middle is never final.
The b star needs at least one b.
Every string of this expression ends with which letter?
Every string of a, b star, c ends in c. Stopping before the c means rejecting.
An NFA with n states becomes at most two to the n. Why?
n states in the NFA → up to 2ⁿ states in the DFA
Each DFA state is a set of the NFA's states.
Each symbol read doubles the number of states.
Each NFA state has two arrows.
What is each DFA state, on the inside?
Each DFA state is a subset of the n states. And there are two to the n subsets.
With the name rule on top, while became ID. Why?
[a-z]+ return ID;\n"while" return WHILE;
Both match while, and the top one breaks the tie.
The name rule matches more letters.
Flex ignores what is inside quotes.
Count the letters each rule matches.
A tie: both match the whole while. In a tie, the rule on top wins.
Both derivations give the same tree. Why?
Decl ⇒ Tipo Var ; ⇒ … ⇒ float * id ;
They use the same rules, only in another order.
Every grammar gives a single tree per sentence.
The tree only keeps the last step.
Compare the rules each derivation used.
Both use the same rules. The tree shows which rules, not the order of the replacements.
In the fix, the id went to the front. Why?
L → L , id | id becomes L → id L'
The id is the beta, and the list starts with it.
The id is the alpha of the rule.
A terminal always comes first in the fix.
In the original rule, which alternative has no loop?
The beta is the id, the alternative with no loop. Every list starts with it.
Without epsilon in S prime, an if without else disappears. Why?
S → if S S' | x S' → else S | ε
S' must be able to become nothing after if S.
The ε marks the end of the input in an if without else.
Every new rule needs an ε.
In an if without else, what must S prime generate?
In an if without else, nothing comes after if S. Only epsilon lets S prime become nothing.
At the end of the input, the table used R goes to epsilon. Why?
top: R input: $
$ is in FOLLOW of R.
At the end of the input, any rule will do.
R goes to ε is the default rule.
The cell of R with dollar came from FOLLOW of R.
Dollar can come after R. So the cell R with dollar tells R to vanish.
R calls R again, and still it does not loop forever. Why?
void R() { if (tok == ',') { casa(','); casa(ID); R(); } }
R matches the comma and the id before calling itself.
Right recursion is never called.
The compiler limits the calls.
What does R do before calling itself?
Before calling R again, it matches the comma and the id. The input moves on every call.
At the second error, the parser popped Val instead of discarding. Why?
top: Val token: ;
The ; is in FOLLOW of Val.
A semicolon is never discarded.
Val had been on top for a long time.
Can the semicolon come after Val?
The semicolon comes after Val. So the parser gives up on Val and moves on.
With the input open parenthesis, id, the parser rejects. Why?
stack: ( S input: $
Without the ), ( S never forms a handle.
Every input with a parenthesis is rejected.
The id cannot become S.
Which rule ends with a closing parenthesis?
The rule needs the closing parenthesis at the end. Without it, the stack never reduces to a single S.
With left on minus, five minus two minus one gave two. Why?
Left says to reduce 5 - 2 first.
Left makes Bison read from the left.
Left makes minus stronger than times.
In the conflict, does left say shift or reduce?
Left says reduce. Five minus two becomes three first, and three minus one gives two.
Integer plus real gave real, with no error. Why?
int + float → float
The integer becomes real before the sum.
Real beats any other type.
The compiler ignores the type of the sum.
Can an integer be written as a real without losing anything?
An integer fits in a real without losing anything. The compiler converts it, and the sum becomes real.
In x equals x plus one, the lookup stopped at the inner table. Why?
inner: x float\nouter: z int, x float
The lookup starts at the inner block.
The inner table is always the biggest.
The lookup always ends at the global table.
In which table does the lookup start?
The lookup starts at the top of the stack, the inner block. The x is there, so it stops.
The times became the last operation, t3. Why?
It needs t1 and t2 to be ready.
Times always comes last.
t3 was the only free temporary.
What does the times sign need for its operation?
The times sign uses t1 and t2. It only runs after both exist.
Ten minus six could only be folded after two times three. Why?
Before that, an operation stood where the six is.
Minus always waits for times.
The compiler folds from right to left.
Before the first fold, what stood where the six is?
Before that, an operation stood where the six is. Only a number with a number can be folded.
After h and g returned, f ran again. Why?
stack: main, f
The record of f is back on top.
h called f at the end.
main called f one more time.
Who was left on top when g left?
When g leaves, the record of f is back on top. It goes on from where it stopped.
Liveness started from the last line. Why?
live = will still be read later on
Live depends on the reads that come later.
The last line uses more temporaries.
The program runs from bottom to top.
Live means it will still be read. Where are those reads?
The reads that matter are further down. Starting from the end, each line already knows what comes next.
